::: {.chapter-lead}
This page is an **advanced deep dive** into [scaled dot-product attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd). It develops a question the main lesson covers in one sentence: why divide the scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$, and how far does that justification hold once its assumptions are made explicit?
:::

## Dot-product scale under Gaussian assumptions

Under the simplifying assumption that all query and key components are independent, zero-mean, and unit-variance, their dot product has variance $\sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \operatorname{Var}(q_i k_i) = d_k$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{d_k}$: for $d_k=64$, it is 8. Large differences between scores in a row can concentrate softmax and reduce its gradients. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ reduces this risk in the simplified model; neither saturation nor its absence is guaranteed for learned projections.

::: {.micro-workbench}
::: {.micro-workbench-header}
<span>NUMERICAL WORKBENCH · SCORE SCALE</span>
<span>Python 3.12+ / NumPy</span>
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-body}
```python
import numpy as np

### Simulate dot products for d_k = 64
np.random.seed(42)
d_k = 64
N = 10000

### Independent standard normal random vectors
q = np.random.randn(N, d_k)
k = np.random.randn(N, d_k)

### Raw dot products q . k
raw_dots = np.sum(q * k, axis=1)

### Compare raw vs scaled standard deviation
std_raw = np.std(raw_dots)
std_scaled = np.std(raw_dots / np.sqrt(d_k))

print(f"Raw std dev: {std_raw:.2f} (theoretical: {np.sqrt(d_k):.1f})")
print(f"Scaled std dev: {std_scaled:.2f} (theoretical: 1.0)")

assert np.isclose(std_scaled, 1.0, atol=0.05)
```
:::
::: {.micro-workbench-footer}
In this simulation, dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings score variance approximately to one. It measures neither softmax weights nor gradients.
:::
:::

## What happens to the scaling factor as $d_k$ grows?

<details class="spot-the-fallacy">
<summary>Common Fallacy: “Increasing head dimension $d_k$ automatically improves attention expressiveness with no drawbacks”</summary>
<div class="fallacy-content">
<p><strong>Limitation:</strong> Under the assumptions above and without scaling, increasing $d_k$ from 64 to 512 multiplies score standard deviation by $\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$. Larger score differences can concentrate softmax and reduce its local derivatives; this does not prove inevitable saturation or a total halt to learning.</p>
</div>
</details>
